title: Farallón Granate (Garnet Rock Ridge)
altText: A tall, three-dimensional fiber artwork made of wrapped wool and horsehair. It is textile rather than a flat picture, and its title suggests a rocky ridge in a garnet color.

source.verifiedBy: Art Institute of Chicago API record: title, artist, date, medium, dimensions (172.7 x 78.7 x 114 cm), credit line, classification (textile, weaving, fiber art), is_public_domain false and image alt text read from the record

context: Olga de Amaral is a Colombian artist, born in 1932, who works with fiber. This 1973 work is made of wool and horsehair using a wrapping technique, and it measures about 173 centimeters tall and 114 centimeters deep, so it extends into the space around it.

descriptions.k: This is not a flat picture. It is made of thread and hair, wrapped and woven. It stands tall. The title says it is like a rock ridge. Would you want to touch it? What would it feel like?
descriptions.g12: Olga de Amaral is an artist from Colombia. She made this art from wool and horsehair, wrapped and woven. It is about as tall as a grown person and sticks out into the room. The title means Garnet Rock Ridge. What do you think a ridge made of thread would be like?
descriptions.g35: Olga de Amaral, an artist from Colombia, made Farallón Granate in 1973 from wool and horsehair that were wrapped and woven. It is about 173 centimeters tall and 114 centimeters deep, so it is more like a sculpture than a flat picture. The title means Garnet Rock Ridge. How does the artist make soft thread look like it could be a mountain or rock?
descriptions.g68: Olga de Amaral is a Colombian artist known for fiber art. In 1973 she made Farallón Granate (Garnet Rock Ridge) from wool and horsehair, using a wrapping technique. At about 173 by 79 by 114 centimeters, it stands in space like a sculpture rather than hanging flat like a painting. The title evokes a rocky ridge in garnet red. Notice how a soft, handmade material can suggest something hard and monumental.
descriptions.g910: Farallón Granate (Garnet Rock Ridge), from 1973, shows Olga de Amaral expanding weaving into sculptural space. Wool and horsehair are wrapped rather than simply woven, and the work measures about 173 by 79 by 114 centimeters, so it occupies a volume of its own. The title points to a rocky ridge, linking soft fiber to geology and landscape. By treating textile as a primary art form, Amaral challenges the old divide between craft and fine art.
descriptions.g1112: Olga de Amaral's 1973 Farallón Granate (Garnet Rock Ridge) uses wrapped wool and horsehair to create a work that stands between textile, sculpture, and landscape evocation. At roughly 173 by 79 by 114 centimeters, it occupies space rather than hanging as a surface, and its title links soft materials to the idea of a rock ridge. The work can be read within the history of fiber art, which challenged the hierarchy of craft and painting, and within Latin American modernism, though the record leaves the artist's intentions for this piece open.

teacherNote.context: Made in 1973 by Colombian artist Olga de Amaral from wool and horsehair using wrapping. The record lists dimensions of about 173 by 79 by 114 centimeters. Check the image before classroom use, since only metadata was read.
directions: Have students wrap yarn around cardboard or tubes to build a small three-dimensional form and describe what it suggests.
Ask students to compare a soft material and a hard material and discuss what happens when an artist makes one resemble the other.
Discuss why some art forms have been called craft rather than art, and who decides.
